content: The references provided include a wide range of systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and guideline documents that address various aspects of physical activity, sedentary behavior, and their impacts on health outcomes across different populations. 1. The World Health Organization (WHO) published recommendations in 2016 on antenatal care aimed at ensuring a positive pregnancy experience. These guidelines emphasize evidence-based practices to improve maternal and fetal health outcomes. 2. The WHO Handbook for Guideline Development (2nd edition, 2014) provides a comprehensive framework for creating evidence-based health guidelines, ensuring methodological rigor and transparency. 3. Poitras et al. (2016) conducted a systematic review examining the relationships between objectively measured physical activity and various health indicators in school-aged children and youth. The findings highlight the importance of physical activity for physical and mental health. 4. Tremblay et al. (2016) developed Canadian 24-hour movement guidelines for children and youth, integrating recommendations on physical activity, sedentary behavior, and sleep to promote overall health and well-being. 5. Carson et al. (2016) updated a systematic review on the associations between sedentary behavior and health indicators in school-aged children and youth, emphasizing the negative health impacts of prolonged sedentary time. 6. Okely et al. (2019) introduced Australian 24-hour movement guidelines for children and young people, integrating physical activity, sedentary behavior, and sleep recommendations to support healthy development. 7. Mottola et al. (2019) published Canadian guidelines on physical activity during pregnancy, providing evidence-based recommendations to optimize maternal and fetal health outcomes. 8. Davenport et al. (2019) conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis demonstrating that prenatal exercise is not associated with an increased risk of fetal mortality, supporting its safety during pregnancy. 9. Davenport et al. (2018) reviewed the effects of prenatal exercise on reducing prenatal and postnatal anxiety and depressive symptoms, highlighting its mental health benefits for pregnant individuals. 10. Davenport et al. (2018) examined the impact of prenatal exercise on neonatal and childhood outcomes, finding positive associations with improved health metrics. 11. Davenport et al. (2018) reviewed the role of prenatal exercise in preventing gestational diabetes mellitus and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, demonstrating its protective effects. 12. Davenport et al. (2019) analyzed the impact of prenatal exercise on maternal harms, labor, and delivery outcomes, concluding that exercise is generally safe and beneficial. 13. Davenport et al. (2019) investigated the effects of prenatal exercise on the incidence of congenital anomalies and hyperthermia, finding no significant risks associated with exercise. 14. Ruchat et al. (2018) reviewed the effectiveness of exercise interventions in preventing excessive gestational weight gain and postpartum weight retention, supporting the role of physical activity in weight management during and after pregnancy. 15. The Physical Activity Guidelines Advisory Committee (2018) released a scientific report summarizing the evidence on physical activity and its health benefits, forming the basis for updated U.S. guidelines. 16. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (2018) published the second edition of the Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, providing evidence-based recommendations for all age groups. 17. Sherrington et al. (2019) conducted a Cochrane review on exercise interventions for preventing falls in older adults living in the community, demonstrating the effectiveness of targeted exercise programs. 18. Wijndaele et al. (2015) reviewed the utilization and harmonization of accelerometry data in adults, providing expert consensus on its application in physical activity research. 19. Guyatt et al. (2008) introduced the GRADE framework for rating the quality of evidence and strength of recommendations, which has become a standard in evidence-based medicine. 20. Shea et al. (2017) developed AMSTAR 2, a critical appraisal tool for systematic reviews that include randomized or non-randomized studies of healthcare interventions. 21. Wells et al. (2017) described the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) for assessing the quality of non-randomized studies in meta-analyses, widely used in observational research. 22. Cillekens et al. (2020) conducted an umbrella review on the health effects of occupational physical activity, summarizing findings from 158 observational studies on 23 health outcomes. 23. Lang et al. (submitted) reviewed the adverse effects of leisure-time physical activity on injury risk and osteoarthritis in adults, summarizing evidence from 14 systematic reviews. 24. Schuch et al. (2019) performed a meta-analysis showing that physical activity protects against incident anxiety, based on prospective cohort studies. 25. Schuch et al. (2018) demonstrated through a meta-analysis that physical activity reduces the risk of incident depression, emphasizing its mental health benefits. 26. Brasure et al. (2018) reviewed the role of physical activity interventions in preventing cognitive decline and Alzheimer-type dementia, highlighting their potential in maintaining cognitive health. 27. Northey et al. (2018) conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on the effects of exercise interventions on cognitive function in adults over 50, showing significant benefits. 28. Engeroff et al. (2018) reviewed the impact of lifelong physical activity on domain-specific cognitive function in older adults, emphasizing the importance of sustained activity. 29. Rathore and Lom (2017) analyzed the effects of chronic and acute physical activity on working memory performance, based on randomized controlled trials. 30. Gordon et al. (2018) conducted a meta-analysis on the efficacy of resistance exercise training in reducing depressive symptoms, supporting its role in mental health management. 31. Gordon et al. (2017) reviewed the effects of resistance exercise training on anxiety, demonstrating its effectiveness in reducing symptoms. 32. Perez-Lopez et al. (2017) analyzed the effects of programmed exercise on depressive symptoms in midlife and older women, showing significant improvements. 33. Moore et al. (2012) conducted a pooled cohort analysis on the relationship between moderate-to-vigorous leisure-time physical activity and mortality, demonstrating a dose-response effect. 34. Arem et al. (2015) provided a detailed pooled analysis of the dose-response relationship between leisure-time physical activity and mortality, supporting its protective effects. 35. Jakicic et al. (2018) reviewed the association between bout duration of physical activity and health outcomes, emphasizing the benefits of even short bouts of activity. 36. Saint-Maurice et al. (2018) examined whether the duration of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity bouts affects all-cause mortality, finding that total activity matters more than bout length. 37. Stamatakis et al. (2018) analyzed the unique health benefits of strength-promoting exercise, showing its association with reduced all-cause, cancer, and cardiovascular mortality. 38. Dinu et al. (2019) reviewed the health outcomes associated with active commuting, highlighting its benefits for multiple health metrics. These references collectively underscore the critical role of physical activity in promoting physical, mental, and cognitive health across the lifespan, while also addressing the risks associated with sedentary behavior.
